rationale: B wins because it finds the more reportable cut inside the announcement: "Why local-currency reimbursement is the hard part of going global, not the card itself" gives a real sub-beat, a mechanics question, and proof a reporter can chase. A is strong, but "The corporate-card feature CFOs of global startups actually asked for" leans harder on Brex's own demand claim and starts to sound like dressed-up customer pain. Both know the Ramp angle; B separates category, competition, and infrastructure cleaner.
gaps_in_A: "Brex spends big on global infrastructure without saying if it's profitable" asserts spending scale without a cost, burn, hiring, or partner-investment fact. The scrutiny angle is useful; the headline overstates the record.
"The corporate-card feature CFOs of global startups actually asked for" leans hard on "top enterprise customer request" and "venture-backed startups" without a named CFO or customer proof.

"Brex's global card rollout is a bet that expense software has to go everywhere its customers do" and the CFO-pain angle share too much of the same buyer-globalization spine; distinct enough, not crisp enough.
gaps_in_B: "because enterprises asked for one global spend stack" smuggles in "one global spend stack" beyond the supplied facts. It may be true; it is not proven.
"the category is consolidating from per-region tools into a single global stack" is a market thesis, not a fact in the update. Needs outside evidence before it leaves the room.
"FX, compliance, and settlement problem more than a card-issuance one" is smart but inferential. Label it as the reporting question, not the conclusion.
It leaves the $12.3B/private-held/profitability thread in questions instead of making a disciplined financial-scrutiny angle from facts the brief plainly supplied.
